paraphrase: Because one is struck by the three kinds of suffering, there arises the desire to know the means of striking them down. If it is objected that the inquiry is pointless because visible means exist, (the answer is) no, because those means do not remove suffering with certainty or finally.

original.text: duḥkhatrayābhighātāj jijñāsā tadabhighātake hetau / dṛṣṭe sāpārthā cen naikāntātyantato 'bhāvāt
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The verse says only 'the three sufferings'; the names ādhyātmika, ādhibhautika, ādhidaivika are supplied by the commentaries (Gauḍapāda, Māṭhara, Vācaspati). Variant: tad-apaghātake / tad-avaghātake.

paraphrase: The means known from Vedic tradition (ānuśravika) are like the visible means, for they are bound up with impurity, decay and gradation. The opposite means is better: the discriminating knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest and the knower.

original.text: dṛṣṭavad ānuśravikaḥ sa hy aviśuddhikṣayātiśayayuktaḥ / tadviparītaḥ śreyān vyaktāvyaktajñavijñānāt
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators explain the impurity (aviśuddhi) as arising from the killing of animals in sacrifice (Gauḍapāda, Vācaspati). Māṭhara reads 'aviśuddhaḥ kṣayātiśayayuktaḥ'.

paraphrase: Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven beginning with the great one (mahat) are both producers and modifications; the group of sixteen is modification only; puruṣa is neither producer nor modification.

original.text: mūlaprakṛtir avikṛtir mahadādyāḥ prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ sapta / ṣoḍaśakas tu vikāro na prakṛtir na vikṛtiḥ puruṣaḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Three means of valid knowledge are accepted — perception, inference and reliable testimony — since every other means is established within these; for what is to be known is established through a means of knowledge.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Perception is the determination (adhyavasāya) concerning each (sense-)object; inference is declared to be threefold and preceded by (knowledge of) the mark and what bears the mark; reliable testimony is reliable revelation (āptaśruti).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The three kinds of inference are named by the commentators (pūrvavat, śeṣavat, sāmānyatodṛṣṭa); Vācaspati also divides inference into vīta and avīta.

paraphrase: Things beyond the senses are known through inference from general correlation (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa); what is imperceptible and not established even by that is established by reliable scripture.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variants: prasiddhir for pratītir; sādhyam for siddham.

paraphrase: (Existing things are not perceived) because of excessive distance, excessive nearness, impairment of the senses, inattention of the mind, subtlety, obstruction, being overpowered, and mixture with what is similar.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Its (prakṛti's) non-perception is due to subtlety, not to non-existence; it is apprehended through its effects. That effect is the great one (mahat) and the rest, unlike prakṛti and also like it.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The effect exists (in its cause before production): because the non-existent cannot be produced; because a definite material cause is taken up; because not everything arises from everything; because a capable cause produces only what it is capable of producing; and because the effect has the nature of its cause.

original.text: asadakaraṇād upādānagrahaṇāt sarvasaṃbhavābhāvāt / śaktasya śakyakaraṇāt kāraṇabhāvāc ca satkāryam
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The manifest has a cause, is impermanent, non-pervasive, active, many, dependent (on its cause), a mark (that merges back), composed of parts and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The manifest consists of the three guṇas, is non-discriminating, an object, common, unconscious and productive; so too is pradhāna. Puruṣa is the opposite of these, and also (in other respects) similar.

original.text: triguṇam aviveki viṣayaḥ sāmānyam acetanaṃ prasavadharmi / vyaktaṃ tathā pradhānaṃ tadviparītas tathā ca pumān
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators explain puruṣa's similarity as sharing with the unmanifest the properties of being uncaused, eternal, pervasive etc. (cf. SK 10).

paraphrase: The guṇas have the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion; they serve to illuminate, to activate and to restrain; and they function by dominating, supporting and producing one another and by being paired together.

original.text: prītyaprītiviṣādātmakāḥ prakāśapravṛttiniyamārthāḥ / anyonyābhibhavāśrayajananamithunavṛttayaś ca guṇāḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas stimulating and mobile; tamas heavy and enveloping. Their functioning (together) serves a purpose, like a lamp.

original.text: sattvaṃ laghu prakāśakam iṣṭam upaṣṭambhakaṃ calaṃ ca rajaḥ / guru varaṇakam eva tamaḥ pradīpavac cārthato vṛttiḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators explain the lamp: oil, wick and flame, though opposed, together give light.

paraphrase: Non-discrimination and the other properties (of the manifest) are established because it consists of the three guṇas and their opposite is absent (in it); the unmanifest too is established, because an effect has the nature of the guṇas of its cause.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The first half has several variant readings (see Ruzsa's apparatus).

paraphrase: (The unmanifest exists as cause) because particular things are limited in measure; because of their homogeneity; because activity proceeds from a potency; because cause and effect are distinguished; and because the whole manifold world merges back (into non-distinction).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The unmanifest exists as cause. It operates through the three guṇas, by their combination and by transformation, like water, (becoming different) according to the differences of the abodes of the respective guṇas.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Water is the commentators' image of rain, one in taste, becoming different in different receptacles.

paraphrase: Puruṣa exists: because aggregates are for the sake of another; because there must be something opposite to what has the three guṇas and the rest; because there must be a controller; because there is an enjoyer; and because activity is for the sake of isolation.

original.text: saṃghātaparārthatvāt triguṇādiviparyayād adhiṣṭhānāt / puruṣo 'sti bhoktṛbhāvāt kaivalyārthaṃ pravṛtteś ca
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The plurality of puruṣas is established: because birth, death and the instruments are allotted to each separately; because (beings) do not act all at once; and because of differences in the (proportion of the) three guṇas.

original.text: jananamaraṇakaraṇānāṃ pratiniyamād ayugapatpravṛtteś ca / puruṣabahutvaṃ siddhaṃ traiguṇyaviparyayāc caiva
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variant: janma- for janana-.

paraphrase: And from that contrast (with the guṇas) it is established that this puruṣa is witness, isolated, neutral, seer and non-agent.

original.text: tasmāc ca viparyāsāt siddhaṃ sākṣitvam asya puruṣasya / kaivalyaṃ mādhyasthyaṃ draṣṭṛtvam akartṛbhāvaś ca
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Therefore, from conjunction with it (puruṣa), the unconscious subtle body (liṅga) appears as if conscious; and though agency belongs to the guṇas, the indifferent one (puruṣa) appears as if the agent.

original.text: tasmāt tatsaṃyogād acetanaṃ cetanāvad iva liṅgam / guṇakartṛtve ca tathā karteva bhavaty udāsīnaḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The conjunction of the two — for the sake of seeing (named with puruṣa) and for the sake of isolation (named with pradhāna) — is like that of the lame man and the blind man; creation is produced by it.

original.text: puruṣasya darśanārthaṃ kaivalyārthaṃ tathā pradhānasya / paṅgvandhavad ubhayor api saṃyogas tatkṛtaḥ sargaḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators construe the genitives differently (e.g., Vācaspati: for pradhāna to be seen by puruṣa, and for puruṣa's isolation).

paraphrase: From prakṛti (arises) the great one (mahat); from that, the I-maker (ahaṃkāra); from that, the group of sixteen; and from five among those sixteen, the five gross elements.

original.text: prakṛter mahāṃs tato 'haṃkāras tasmād gaṇaś ca ṣoḍaśakaḥ / tasmād api ṣoḍaśakāt pañcabhyaḥ pañca bhūtāni
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Buddhi is determination (adhyavasāya). Virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power are its sāttvika form; its tāmasa form is the reverse of these.

original.text: adhyavasāyo buddhir dharmo jñānaṃ virāga aiśvaryam / sāttvikam etad rūpaṃ tāmasam asmād viparyastam
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Ahaṃkāra is self-assertion (abhimāna). From it a twofold creation proceeds: the group of eleven (organs) and the group of five subtle elements.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The sāttvika group of eleven proceeds from ahaṃkāra as modified (vaikṛta); the subtle elements from (ahaṃkāra as) bhūtādi, which is tāmasa; both (groups) from (ahaṃkāra as) taijasa.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The sense capacities (buddhīndriya) are named ear, skin, eye, tongue and nose; speech, hands, feet, anus and genitals are called the capacities of action (karmendriya).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The order of the sense capacities differs between recensions.

paraphrase: Here mind (manas) partakes of both (kinds); it constructs (saṅkalpaka) and is a capacity (indriya) by similarity (with the others). The diversity (of the organs) comes from particular transformations of the guṇas and from the differences of external objects.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: V2 and the Yuktidīpikā read a different verse here (mind as instrument of both kinds, internal, of the three times).

paraphrase: The function of the five (sense capacities) with regard to sound and the rest is mere awareness (ālocana); speaking, grasping, walking, excreting and delight are (the functions) of the (other) five.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variant: rūpādiṣu for śabdādiṣu.

paraphrase: The (three internal organs) each have their own characteristic function, which is not shared; the shared function of the instruments is the five vital winds, prāṇa and the rest.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: With regard to what is perceived, the functioning of the four (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas and a sense) is taught to be simultaneous and also successive; with regard to what is not perceived, the functioning of the three is preceded by that.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The instruments take up their own functions prompted by one another's impulse; puruṣa's purpose alone is the cause; the instrument is not made to act by anyone.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The instrument is of thirteen kinds; it seizes, holds and illuminates; its object is tenfold — what is to be seized, held and illuminated.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The internal instrument is threefold, the external tenfold, called the objects (i.e., presenting objects) of the three. The external operates in present time; the internal instrument in all three times.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Of these, the five sense capacities have specific and non-specific objects; speech has sound as its object; the rest (of the action capacities) have all five objects.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Since buddhi together with the internal organs apprehends every object, the threefold instrument is the door-keeper and the rest are the doors.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: These (organs), particular modifications of the guṇas, differing from one another, illuminate like lamps the whole purpose of puruṣa and present it to buddhi.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Because buddhi accomplishes every experience of puruṣa, it is also buddhi that discriminates the subtle difference between pradhāna and puruṣa.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The subtle elements are non-specific; from these five come the five gross elements; these are called specific, and they are calm, turbulent and dull.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Subtle (bodies), (bodies) born of mother and father, and the gross elements: these are the three kinds of specifics. Of these the subtle are constant; those born of mother and father perish.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The subtle body (liṅga) — produced first, unattached, constant, (made of the principles) from mahat down to the subtle elements — transmigrates, without enjoyment (of its own), perfumed by the dispositions (bhāva).

original.text: pūrvotpannam asaktaṃ niyataṃ mahadādisūkṣmaparyantam / saṃsarati nirupabhogaṃ bhāvair adhivāsitaṃ liṅgam
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: As a picture does not stand without a support, or a shadow without a post and the like, so the subtle body does not subsist without a support, without the specifics.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Some editions read 'without the non-specifics' (vinā 'viśeṣaiḥ).

paraphrase: Motivated by the purpose of puruṣa, this subtle body, through the connection of occasioning causes and their results and through the pervasive power of prakṛti, plays its parts like an actor.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The dispositions — virtue and the rest — are seen to be innate, natural and acquired; they rest on the instrument (buddhi), while the embryonic stages beginning with the kalala rest on the effect (the body).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Through virtue there is upward movement, through non-virtue downward movement; through knowledge, liberation; through the reverse, bondage is held to follow.

original.text: dharmeṇa gamanam ūrdhvaṃ gamanam adhastād bhavaty adharmeṇa / jñānena cāpavargo viparyayād iṣyate bandhaḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Through dispassion, absorption into prakṛti; through passion of the nature of rajas, saṃsāra; through power, non-obstruction; through their reverse, the reverse.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Commentators explain: dispassion without knowledge of the principles leads to absorption in prakṛti, not to liberation.

paraphrase: This is the creation of cognitions (pratyaya-sarga), called error, incapacity, contentment and accomplishment; through the suppression (of one guṇa by another) due to the inequality of the guṇas, its divisions are fifty.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: There are five kinds of error; of incapacity, due to defects of the instruments, twenty-eight kinds; contentment is ninefold, accomplishment eightfold.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Darkness (tamas) has eight divisions, and so has delusion (moha); great delusion is tenfold; gloom (tāmisra) is eighteenfold, and so is blind gloom (andhatāmisra).
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Incapacity is declared to be the injuries of the eleven organs together with the injuries of buddhi; the injuries of buddhi are seventeen, through the reversal of the contentments and accomplishments.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Nine contentments are declared: four internal, called nature, means, time and fortune; and five external, arising from abstention from (the five) objects.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variant: abhimatāḥ / abhihitāḥ.

paraphrase: Reasoning, (hearing) words, study, the three destructions of suffering, gaining friends, and giving are the eight accomplishments; the preceding three (error, incapacity, contentment) are the threefold curb of accomplishment.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Without the dispositions there is no subtle body; without the subtle body the dispositions do not come about; hence creation is twofold, called that of the liṅga and that of the dispositions.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: The divine (creation) is of eight kinds, the animal of five, and the human of one kind; this in brief is the creation of beings.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Above, (creation) abounds in sattva; at the root, in tamas; in the middle, in rajas — from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: There the conscious puruṣa undergoes suffering produced by old age and death, until the subtle body ceases; hence suffering is by nature.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variant ending samāsena ('in brief') for svabhāvena ('by nature').

paraphrase: Thus this undertaking of prakṛti, from mahat down to the specific elements, is for the liberation of each puruṣa — for another's sake, as if for its own.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: The Yuktidīpikā reads a different first half (pravartate tattvabhūtabhāvākhyaḥ).

paraphrase: As unconscious milk flows for the growth of the calf, so pradhāna acts for the liberation of puruṣa.

original.text: vatsavivṛddhinimittaṃ kṣīrasya yathā pravṛttir ajñasya / puruṣavimokṣanimittaṃ tathā pravṛttiḥ pradhānasya
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: As people engage in actions to satisfy a longing, so the unmanifest acts for the liberation of puruṣa.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: As a dancer, having shown herself to the audience, ceases from dancing, so prakṛti, having shown herself to puruṣa, ceases.

original.text: raṅgasya darśayitvā nivartate nartakī yathā nṛtyāt / puruṣasya tathātmānaṃ prakāśya vinivartate prakṛtiḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: By manifold means prakṛti — helpful, possessed of the guṇas — acts purposelessly (for herself) for the sake of puruṣa, who does not help (her) and is without guṇas.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Nothing, I think, is more modest than prakṛti, who, (knowing) 'I have been seen', does not come into puruṣa's sight again.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Gauḍapāda uses this verse to argue that neither Īśvara, nature nor time, but prakṛti, is the cause.

paraphrase: Therefore no one (no puruṣa) is in truth bound, released, or transmigrates; it is prakṛti, in its various abodes, that transmigrates, is bound and is released.

original.text: tasmān na badhyate 'ddhā na mucyate nāpi saṃsarati kaścit / saṃsarati badhyate mucyate ca nānāśrayā prakṛtiḥ
original.edition: vulgate kārikā text as printed with Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya (Wilson 1837) and with the Māṭhara Vṛtti (Chowkhamba 1970), checked against the GRETIL e-texts incl. F. Ruzsa's edition with variants
original.licence: ancient text (public domain); e-text consulted for reference only

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Māṭhara reads 'nāpi mucyate' for ''ddhā na mucyate'.

paraphrase: Prakṛti binds herself by herself by means of seven forms; and for the sake of puruṣa she releases herself by means of one form.

original.text: rūpaiḥ saptabhir eva tu badhnāty ātmānam ātmanā prakṛtiḥ / saiva ca puruṣārthaṃ prati vimocayaty ekarūpeṇa

notes: The seven forms are virtue, non-virtue, ignorance, dispassion, passion, power and non-power; the one form is knowledge (commentators). This verse is missing in Paramārtha's Chinese version.

paraphrase: Thus, from repeated practice of the principles, there arises the knowledge 'I am not, (nothing is) mine, not I' — complete, pure because free from error, and single (kevala).

original.text: evaṃ tattvābhyāsān nāsmi na me nāham ity apariśeṣam / aviparyayād viśuddhaṃ kevalam utpadyate jñānam

speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa

paraphrase: Through that (knowledge) puruṣa, like a spectator, at ease, sees prakṛti, which has ceased to produce and, through the force of the purpose (fulfilled), has turned away from the seven forms.
speaker: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
notes: Variants: svasthaḥ / susthaḥ / svacchaḥ.

paraphrase: One (puruṣa), (thinking) 'I have seen her', is indifferent; the other, (thinking) 'I have been seen', ceases. Though their conjunction remains, there is no motive for (further) creation.

original.text: dṛṣṭā mayety upekṣaka eko dṛṣṭāham ity uparamaty anyā / sati saṃyoge 'pi tayoḥ prayojanaṃ nāsti sargasya

paraphrase: When perfect knowledge has been attained, so that virtue and the rest cease to be causes, (the knower) remains, bearing a body, through the force of latent impressions, like the whirling of a potter's wheel.

original.text: samyagjñānādhigamād dharmādīnām akāraṇaprāptau / tiṣṭhati saṃskāravaśāc cakrabhramavad dhṛtaśarīraḥ

paraphrase: When separation from the body is attained and pradhāna ceases because its purpose has been fulfilled, he attains isolation that is both certain and final.

paraphrase: This secret knowledge for the purpose of puruṣa has been expounded by the supreme sage; in it the persistence, origination and dissolution of beings are considered.

paraphrase: This supreme purifier the sage gave out of compassion to Āsuri; Āsuri (gave it) to Pañcaśikha, by whom the doctrine was expanded.
